A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same K-Prism research. Text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable, supporting reliable comparison after matching relocated content.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation experiments across 18 datasets, baseline comparisons, component ablations and supplementary analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds baseline evaluations, throughput measurements, reference-sensitivity studies and failure examples.

M1.justification: The dual-prompt representation, three operating modes, MoE decoder, training losses and inference procedures are unchanged. Section 3 and Appendix A.3 retain the same architecture; additional reference-count experiments evaluate its existing capabilities.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 12 training datasets, four external datasets and two unseen-class datasets for the same segmentation tasks. New analyses reuse this coverage; varying reference counts changes experimental settings.

E2.justification: v2 broadens two main comparisons: Tables 2–3 add task-specific nnU-Net alongside universal semantic models, while Table 4 and Figures 3, 5 and 8 add MedSAM to interactive comparisons. Both methods were already cited in v1 but absent from these evaluated comparator sets. Existing baselines remain.

E3.justification: Core splits, preprocessing, training budgets and segmentation metrics remain unchanged. Appendix A.4 introduces single-A100 throughput evaluation with one to five experts, randomized reference-selection evaluations, and 1/3/5/9-shot AMOS MRI testing with specified axial sampling locations. These are additional protocols, not revisions of the original benchmark settings.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained ablations in Tables 5 and 7, v2 adds computational-cost analysis in Table 8, reference-selection sensitivity on ACDC/BUS in Table 9, reference-quantity sensitivity on AMOS MRI in Table 10, and BraTS/M&Ms-2 failure cases in Appendix A.6 and Figure 9. These substantially broaden investigation of robustness and practical limitations.

E5.justification: New Table 9 reports means, standard deviations and minimum–maximum values across ten independent one-shot evaluations using different references per dataset. v1 lacks this variability analysis. This concerns reference selection, not repeated training seeds; uncertainty reporting for the main comparisons remains unchanged.

E6.justification: Existing benchmark and ablation values are retained, while substantial additional outcomes are reported. New nnU-Net averages are 81.00% and 74.92% in Tables 2–3; MedSAM five-click Dice scores are 91.21%, 90.93% and 80.13% across Table 4's groups. Tables 8–10 add throughput, reference variability and few-shot results, including 79.90% Dice with nine references versus the retained 78.21% one-shot result. Figure 9 adds failure examples.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and derivations, including Equations 1–23 in Section 3 and Appendix A.3, are unchanged. No new formal assumptions, theorems or proofs are introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same claims: unifying three knowledge paradigms through dual prompts and an MoE decoder, with state-of-the-art performance and generalization across 18 datasets. Additional evidence does not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: Section 5 and Appendix A.6 substantially expand explanations of appearance-matching failures under anatomical shifts and why interactive refinement can remain effective. They elaborate the limitations of 2D context and possible volumetric propagation. Appendix A.4 adds interpretations of reference robustness and computational cost, including a new multi-GPU scaling claim; A.8 explicitly restricts intended use to research pending clinical validation.

D1.justification: v2 replaces promised future code release with a repository address and stated public availability. Appendix A.2 newly specifies SAM2 checkpoint initialization, MAE-pretrained ViT-Base initialization for SegNext/MedSAM, scratch training for models such as MultiverSeg, and consistent click simulation. New studies disclose hardware and reference-sampling details. These disclosures do not establish changes to existing experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds Liu et al. (2024b) on multi-organ segmentation and Yousef et al. (2023) on brain tumors to support added discussion. Main related-work positioning remains unchanged. Consolidating Verse's preprint citation into its already cited publication does not remove a distinct work.

P1.justification: There are localized result/discussion rewrites, expanded appendix explanations, and new acknowledgments, failure-analysis, ethics and reproducibility sections. Author affiliations and publication headers are updated. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Visual evidence is substantially expanded with Tables 8–10 and failure-case Figure 9. Tables 2–3 distinguish task-specific and universal models; Table 4 and Figures 3, 5 and 8 incorporate MedSAM. Convergence plots are redrawn with stronger lines, expanded legends and revised vertical-axis ranges, alongside relocation of existing displays.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens an already extensive evaluation through additional baselines, reference-sensitivity measurements and explicit failure cases, while improving reproducibility documentation and reported code access. These additions make the unchanged central results easier to assess. The gain is tempered by limited uncertainty coverage and the new assertion of near-linear multi-GPU scaling and real-time usability, which the single-GPU measurements in Table 8 do not establish.
